title: The Architecture of Waiting Rooms
dek: Airports, hospitals, motor vehicle offices — the rooms we build for people who are, by design, doing nothing. A short study of the furniture of delay.
body: There is a particular chair, bolted in a row of five, upholstered in a color that exists nowhere else in the visible world. You have sat in it. It was designed by someone who was told, explicitly, that comfort past twenty minutes was not a requirement worth solving for.

Waiting rooms are the only interiors built around an absence — the person who isn't ready for you yet. Everything in them is a negotiation with that absence: the clock placed where you'll see it but can't quite read the second hand, the magazines eighteen months out of date, the hush that isn't quite silence.

What's strange is how consistent the vocabulary is, across continents and institutions that share no history. Somewhere, a design decision was made once and never revisited, and now it just is how a waiting room looks. I want to find that first room.

title: On Keeping a Public Notebook
dek: Why this site exists, what it will and won't be, and a small promise about how often I'll update it.
body: This is a notebook, not a publication. There's no editorial calendar, no beat, no obligation to have a take on the news. Some entries will be long. Most won't. A few will just be a link to something I couldn't stop thinking about.
The promise is modest: nothing here is written to perform expertise I don't have. If I'm wrong about something, I'd rather find out from you than pretend otherwise.

title: An Atlas of Countries That Never Existed
dek: A cartographer spent a decade mapping nations from fiction, propaganda, and failed treaties. The maps are gorgeous and slightly unsettling.

title: Interfaces Without Users
dek: Most of the software running today was never meant to be seen. Notes on designing for an audience of other machines.
body: The average interface now has a readership of one program and, if something goes wrong, one tired engineer at 2 a.m. Everyone else in the chain is a machine that will never notice whether the labels are kind.

And yet the good ones are still legible — not to be nice, but because legibility is what lets a human step in without dread when the automated version finally breaks. Designing for machines is still designing for the night someone has to read it by hand.

title: Three Days With a Rotary Phone
dek: I disconnected the smartphone and lived off a 1974 rotary set for a long weekend. Some notes on friction as a feature.
body: Dialing seven digits by hand takes about four seconds — long enough to reconsider the call twice. I didn't expect that pause to be the whole point, but by Saturday it was the only part I missed when I plugged the smartphone back in.

title: The Last Lighthouse Keepers
dek: A quiet, beautifully reported piece on the handful of people still paid to live beside automated lights, just in case.

title: A Taxonomy of Empty Chairs
dek: Boardrooms, courtrooms, thrones: what a room communicates through a chair nobody is sitting in.
body: An empty chair at the head of a table is never neutral. It's a held position, a placeholder for a decision not yet made about who gets to make decisions — and everyone in the room orients around it whether they mean to or not.
Courtrooms formalize this into ritual: you stand for the entrance of no one, because the bench itself outranks whoever will eventually sit in it. The chair was never the point. The waiting was.
